entries.title: 🔢 Sorting by hand - when sorted() is banned
entries.content:
Some subjects forbid sorted() and list.sort(). Insertion sort is short,
stable, and easy to get right under pressure.

```
def my_sort(lst, key=lambda x: x):
    out = list(lst)
    for i in range(1, len(out)):
        cur = out[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and key(out[j]) > key(cur):
            out[j + 1] = out[j]
            j -= 1
        out[j + 1] = cur
    return out
```

Stable means equal elements keep their input order. The strict `>` is what
makes it stable - `>=` would swap equals and break that.

Multi-criteria sorting is just a tuple key:
```
my_sort(words, key=lambda s: (len(s), s.lower(), count_vowels(s)))
```
Tuples compare left to right, so that is "by length, then alphabetically,
then by vowel count" with no extra code.
tips: exam03 py_cryptic_sorter forbids sorted() and list.sort() - this is the exercise
Read the subject for the tie-break rule: 'equal elements keep input order' means you need a STABLE sort
Build the key as a tuple instead of sorting three times
O(n^2) is fine at exam sizes - correctness beats cleverness

entries.title: 🔗 Merging sorted lists - without heapq
entries.content:
Merging two sorted lists is a two-pointer walk:

```
def merge_two(a, b):
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        if a[i] <= b[j]:
            out.append(a[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(b[j]); j += 1
    out.extend(a[i:])
    out.extend(b[j:])
    return out
```

For many lists, fold them one at a time:
```
def merge_all(lists):
    result = []
    for lst in lists:
        result = merge_two(result, lst)
    return result
```

The two `extend` calls at the end are what people forget - one list runs
out before the other and its tail still has to be copied.
tips: exam04 py_merge_sorted_lists forbids sorted(), .sort() AND heapq.merge()
Use <= not < so duplicates are preserved and the merge stays stable
Empty input lists just fall through harmlessly - no special case needed

A self-loop {0: [0]} is a cycle - the colouring catches it for free
Loop over ALL nodes: the graph may be disconnected and the cycle in part 2
GREY vs BLACK is the whole trick - 'already seen' alone gives false positives

entries.title: 🪟 Sliding window & the monotonic deque
entries.content:
The naive max-of-every-window is O(n*k). A deque of INDICES, kept in
decreasing value order, makes it O(n).

```
from collections import deque

def sliding_window_maximum(nums, k):
    if not nums or k <= 0 or k > len(nums):
        return []
    dq, out = deque(), []
    for i, n in enumerate(nums):
        while dq and nums[dq[-1]] <= n:
            dq.pop()
        dq.append(i)
        if dq[0] <= i - k:
            dq.popleft()
        if i >= k - 1:
            out.append(nums[dq[0]])
    return out
```

Any earlier element smaller than what just arrived can never be the max
again - the newcomer outlives it and beats it. So drop them.
The front of the deque is always the current window's maximum.
tips: exam04 py_sliding_window_maximum - guard k <= 0 and k > len(nums), both are tested
Store indices, not values, or you cannot tell when something left the window
dq[0] <= i - k is the 'front has slid out of the window' check

entries.title: 🧮 Dynamic programming - build on smaller answers
entries.content:
DP means: solve prefixes, remember them, and reuse.

Minimum cuts so every piece is a palindrome:
```
def palindrome_partitioner(s):
    n = len(s)
    if n < 2:
        return 0
    pal = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
    cuts = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        best = i                      # worst case: cut before every char
        for j in range(i + 1):
            if s[j] == s[i] and (i - j < 2 or pal[j + 1][i - 1]):
                pal[j][i] = True
                best = 0 if j == 0 else min(best, cuts[j - 1] + 1)
        cuts[i] = best
    return cuts[n - 1]
```

Two tables at once: `pal[j][i]` is "is s[j..i] a palindrome", and
`cuts[i]` is "fewest cuts for the prefix ending at i".
`s[j] == s[i] and pal[j+1][i-1]` is the palindrome recurrence - the ends
match and the inside was already a palindrome.
tips: exam04 py_palindrome_partitioner
If the whole prefix is a palindrome (j == 0) the answer is 0 cuts, not cuts[-1] + 1
i - j < 2 covers the 1 and 2 character cases where there is no inside to check

tips: exam05 py_room_scheduler - sorting by start time first is what makes greedy work

entries.title: 🗺️ Grids & matrices - building and walking them
entries.content:
Build a grid - and beware the aliasing trap:
```
grid = [["."] * n for _ in range(n)]   # correct: n separate rows
grid = [["."] * n] * n                 # WRONG: one row, aliased n times
```
With the wrong one, `grid[0][0] = "*"` changes every row at once.

Direction vectors keep traversal code flat:
```
DIRS4 = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]
DIRS8 = DIRS4 + [(1, 1), (-1, -1), (-1, 1), (1, -1)]

for dx, dy in DIRS8:
    nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy
    if 0 <= ny < len(grid) and 0 <= nx < len(grid[ny]):
        ...
```

Rows back to strings: `["".join(row) for row in grid]`
tips: Negative indices do NOT raise in Python - they wrap. Always bound-check explicitly
Decide up front whether you index [row][col] or [x][y] and write it in a comment
exam04 py_constellation_mapper tests out-of-range AND negative coordinates
Rotate 90 degrees: `[list(r) for r in zip(*grid[::-1])]`

entries.title: 🔤 Characters & ciphers - ord, chr and wrapping
tips: exam03 py_whisper_cipher - non-letters must pass through untouched
Test 'z' with +1 and 'a' with -1: wrapping in both directions is where it breaks
A shift of 26 (or 0) must return the string unchanged

entries.title: 🔟 Number bases & run-length encoding
tips: exam03 py_number_base_converter, exam05 py_compress_decompress
value == 0 needs its own case or the while loop never runs and you return ''
Validate digits against the source base - '2' is not a valid base-2 digit
Decompressing must handle multi-digit counts: 'a12' is twelve a's, not a1 then 2
